recent_posts.title: SQL Commit And Rollback
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide to SQL COMMIT and ROLLBACK transaction control commands covering core syntax across MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server. Topics include ACID properties, autocommit behavior, savepoints for partial rollback, error-handling patterns with TRY/CATCH and exception blocks, stored procedure transaction behavior per engine, real-world retry and batch processing patterns, and production diagnostic queries for identifying long-running or doomed transactions.

recent_posts.title: How To View and Update the Linux PATH Environment Variable
recent_posts.summary: A comprehensive guide to managing the Linux PATH environment variable. Covers viewing PATH with echo and printenv, making temporary changes with export, and persisting changes across bash and zsh via ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, and /etc/environment. Includes a startup file reference table, verification commands (which, type -a, command -v), entry removal with sed, and deduplication guards. Also addresses common production failures: sudo secure_path stripping, SSH non-interactive shells ignoring startup files, stale bash hash caches, cron's minimal PATH, Docker ENV usage, direnv for per-project PATH, macOS path_helper, and systemd service environment isolation.

recent_posts.title: Dedicated vs Serverless Inference as You Scale
recent_posts.summary: Choosing between serverless and dedicated inference isn't a one-time decision — it evolves as your AI system grows. Serverless is ideal early on for its flexibility and zero infrastructure overhead, but as traffic becomes predictable and latency expectations tighten, dedicated GPU infrastructure becomes more cost-effective and performant. The post walks through this lifecycle using a meeting assistant example and compares two platforms: Modal (pure serverless, per-second billing) and Together.ai (serverless-to-dedicated migration without changing code). Key insight: serverless is a phase, not a permanent default. Once workloads stabilize, delaying the move to dedicated infrastructure costs more in both money and performance.

recent_posts.title: Why RAG Systems Fail in Production
recent_posts.summary: RAG systems often work well in demos but degrade in production due to four interconnected failure modes: poor retrieval quality (bad chunking, lack of hybrid retrieval and reranking), latency creep from increasingly complex pipelines, embedding and corpus drift that silently degrades relevance over time, and weak evaluation practices that only measure final answer quality rather than each pipeline stage. The post recommends domain-aware chunking, hybrid dense+sparse retrieval with reranking, versioned embeddings and indexes, separate retrieval and generation metrics (precision@k, recall@k, MRR, groundedness, faithfulness), and continuous monitoring integrated into CI/CD pipelines.

recent_posts.title: Fine-Tuned LLMs on Serverless Architecture
recent_posts.summary: Serverless inference can dramatically cut costs for teams running fine-tuned LLMs by switching from per-hour GPU billing to pay-per-token pricing. The key enabler is Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), specifically LoRA, which produces small adapter weights (10–100 MB) that sit on top of a shared frozen base model. This allows a single GPU to serve hundreds of fine-tuned variants simultaneously via LoRA multiplexing. The article covers the technical mechanics — adapter caching, VRAM management, KV-cache keying, and batching strategies like S-LoRA — as well as practical trade-offs. The main downside is cold starts that spike Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), which can be mitigated with keep-alive requests or lower-rank adapters. The approach is best suited for teams with bursty, inconsistent traffic who want fast deployment without managing GPU infrastructure.

recent_posts.title: The Silent Versioning Problem in AI Inference
recent_posts.summary: AI inference platforms silently change model behavior without notifying developers — through weight updates, infrastructure shifts, quantization changes, or new guardrail layers — all without changing the endpoint name. This creates silent regressions that teams discover from users rather than monitoring. The post examines how major platforms (OpenAI, Anthropic, open-source hosters) handle versioning, documents real-world incidents like the GPT-4o sycophancy rollout and Claude Opus 'nerfing' reports, and outlines coping strategies like snapshot pinning, golden dataset regression testing, and production traffic logging. It argues that platforms should provide full-stack version strings, machine-readable changelogs, reproducibility SLAs, and platform-provided regression testing — and predicts these will become enterprise procurement requirements within 18 months.

recent_posts.title: Post-Inference Storage and Querying with MongoDB
recent_posts.summary: A step-by-step guide to building a FastAPI application that accepts image uploads, stores them in DigitalOcean Spaces, runs vision model inference via the Groq API (using Llama 4 Scout), and persists structured results in MongoDB. Covers MongoDB document schema design with nested inference results, multikey indexes on array fields, dynamic query building with dot notation and $elemMatch for compound array filters, aggregation pipelines for label frequency and average confidence analytics, and FastAPI BackgroundTasks for non-blocking inference processing.

recent_posts.title: The Hidden Bottlenecks in LLM Inference and How to Fix Them
recent_posts.summary: LLM inference performance problems often stem from system design rather than raw hardware. Key bottlenecks include GPU underutilization from heterogeneous request lengths and poor scheduling, memory-bandwidth constraints during the decode phase, and host-side CPU overhead from tokenization and prompt preprocessing. The post explains the prefill vs. decode distinction, why static batching falls short, and how techniques like continuous batching, paged/block-based KV-cache management, prefix caching, and chunked prefill address these issues. A comparison table contrasts traditional vs. modern serving designs (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM), and a practical recommendations table maps specific problems to actionable fixes across metrics, architecture, batching policy, and resource separation.

recent_posts.title: The Hidden Cost of Cold Starts in Serverless AI Workloads
recent_posts.summary: Cold starts in serverless AI workloads introduce significant latency because GPU environments must be provisioned, model weights loaded into VRAM, and frameworks warmed up before inference can begin. For large models (10–15GB+), this can delay first responses by 30–90 seconds, making serverless unsuitable for real-time user-facing applications like chatbots or image generation tools. The post explains why serverless and always-on infrastructure solve fundamentally different problems, walks through a real image generation example comparing both approaches, and outlines mitigation strategies including model preloading, keeping warm instances, hybrid architectures, and switching to persistent GPU instances for latency-sensitive workloads.

recent_posts.title: Comparing purpose-built AI cloud platforms for model training and inference
recent_posts.summary: Purpose-built AI cloud platforms offer compelling alternatives to traditional clouds like AWS and GCP for AI workloads. Five platforms are compared across cost, security, developer experience, and use cases: Baseten (scale-to-zero, regulated industries), Nebius (cheapest always-on H100 at $2.95/hr, strongest compliance), Fireworks AI (fastest inference via FireAttention, Multi-LoRA for per-customer personalization), Modal (best developer experience, per-second billing, Python-first), and Together AI (200+ model catalog, best for exploration and batch workloads). A practical deployment scenario using a fine-tuned Llama model is walked through on each platform. Key finding: none offer complete infrastructure breadth — all require external vector databases and observability tooling — so the right choice depends on matching platform strengths to specific team priorities.
